newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU proposes lower sulphur-in-fuel limit.
newsitem.headline: EU proposes lower sulphur-in-fuel limit.

text.p: The European Commission adopted on Wednesday a proposal to cut the maximum allowed sulphur content in heavy fuel oil to one percent by weight by January 1, 2000, Commission officials told a news conference.
Much of Greece and Portugal, and possibly parts of Italy and Spain, would be exempt from the rules, as would power stations using suitable sulphur-scrubbing equipment.
National markets for heavy fuel oil in the EU also vary widely with Sweden's at 0.3 percent average sulphur content and Spain's at 3.5 percent.

"The present situation is quite a varied picture across the Community. We are talking about some member states who are already at the one percent mark... there are no Community rules on this at the moment," Commission official Jeff Huntington told a news conference.
Exemptions to the heavy fuel oil rules would be allowed "in regions where environmental conditions allow" and for industries which use sulphur-scrubbing technology, the draft text said.
Huntington said the environmental derogation would apply where EU air quality rules were met and where local pollution did not have significant long-distance, transboundary effects.

"As a first estimate... probably most of Portugal and Greece (would qualify), but not the major cities which have air pollution problems. In both these states the contribution to trans-boundary pollution is negligible," he said.
"One can imagine that certain areas or Spain and Italy would (also) fall within that derogation," he added.

The EU executive said costs caused by the draft heavy fuel norms would amount to 760 million European currency units per year, with the major burden falling on refineries (149 million Ecus), power plants (291 million Ecus), transport (49 million Ecus), domestic users (75 million Ecus) and "other industry" (196 million Ecus).
The proposal excludes setting rules for ships' bunker fuels, saying only that international norms should be pursued within ongoing talks within the International Maritime Organisation.

Draft rules -- which come as part of an overall EU strategy intended to cut soil acidification from air-borne pollutants such as sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide and ammonia -- would also allow EU countries to apply stricter norms for gas oil than the current rate of 0.2 percent, officials said.
This would allow countries such as Austria and Sweden to retain existing 0.1 percent limits on gas oil without fear of legal challenge for getting ahead of EU partners with their environmental laws.
"While maintaining the limit, we are opening up for more flexibility for member states who think it's important and relevant to go further," Huntington said.

Swedish Environment Minister Anna Lindh welcomed the move, saying in a statement: "This is an important step to solve one of our most difficult environmental problems and evidence that we can influence the environmental policies of the EU."
The proposal will now go to EU ministers and the European Parliament before final adoption.

Commission data for late 1996 national market averages for the sulphur in heavy fuel oil in the 15 EU countries were: Austria (0.96), Belgium (1.0), Britain (2.18), Denmark (1.0), Finland (1.1), France (2.1), Germany (1.2), Greece (2.7), Ireland (2.0), Italy (1.53), Luxembourg (--), the Netherlands (2.2), Portugal (--), Spain (1 to 3.5 depending on heavy fuel oil type) and Sweden (0.3).
